title: Unit prices: comparing fairly
description: Big packs are not always cheaper and small packs are not always a rip-off. The unit price — cost per 100 grams, per litre, per item — tells you the truth.

body.heading: The small print on the shelf edge
paragraphs: Many supermarkets print a unit price on the shelf label: the cost per 100 grams or per litre, in smaller type beneath the main price. It exists precisely because pack sizes are designed to be hard to compare at a glance.
Try it: 500 grams of pasta at $4 is 80 cents per 100 grams. A 1-kilogram bag at $7 is 70 cents per 100 grams. The big bag wins — but only by 10 cents a unit, and only if you will actually use it all.

body.heading: When the bigger pack loses
paragraphs: Unit price is not the whole story. A cheaper-per-gram pack that goes stale in the cupboard is expensive rubbish. Storage space, shelf life, and your real rate of use all belong in the decision.
Offers complicate it further: a smaller pack on promotion can beat the big pack's unit price for a week. That is why the habit is checking, not assuming in either direction.

body.heading: Beyond the supermarket
paragraphs: The same thinking applies anywhere quantities hide: data plans priced per gigabyte, cleaning products per wash, printer paper per sheet. Whenever a seller emphasises the pack price, quietly ask "per what?"

Unit pricing also exposes the shrinking pack trick, where the price stays the same but the contents quietly get smaller. The unit price rises even when the tag does not — another reason the small print on the shelf edge deserves your attention.

takeaway: Compare cost per 100 grams, per litre, or per use — never just the pack price — and let your storage and appetite have the final vote.
